description: AstroSentinel builds tamper-aware AI health monitoring software for astronauts on deep-space missions. It watches simulated crew vitals, raises medical alerts for real health events like radiation exposure, hypoxia, fever, and cardiac problems, and separately detects cyber attacks on the sensor data, such as spoofed, replayed, or hidden readings. Because crews far from Earth can’t get fast help, they need to trust their health data. Our goal is software that is both smart and secure

details:
High-Level Project Summary

Crews far from Earth can’t get fast medical help, so they must trust their health software. AstroSentinel monitors simulated astronaut vitals and does two jobs: it raises medical alerts for real events (radiation exposure, hypoxia, fever, cardiac problems), and it separately detects cyber attacks on the sensor data (spoofing, drift, replay, stuck sensors, and masking of a real emergency). In tests on a simulated 7-day period, averaged over 5 random simulations, it found about 96% of medical events and 93% of attacks.

Link to Project Demo

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lvl9I-BNZcZK7mnYhGCz3tAMONS45rzs/view?usp=sharing

Link to Final Project

https://github.com/firdausiyamubarak-ux/AstroSentinel-NASA

Detailed Project Description

AstroSentinel responds to the challenge “Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.” NASA’s Human Research Program lists distance from Earth, space radiation and hostile closed environments as spaceflight hazards, and names cardiovascular, immune and hypoxia risks. We simulated 14 days of seven vitals (heart rate, SpO2, respiration, temperature, blood pressure, cabin CO2, radiation dose rate) with events based on these hazards, and injected seven kinds of cyber attack. The software has two layers: a physiology layer (a personal time-of-day baseline plus an Isolation Forest) that finds unusual changes, and an integrity layer (a cross-sensor consistency model, plus flatline and replay checks) that finds data that breaks physiology. Data that is inconsistent is reported as an attack; data that is consistent but abnormal is a medical alert. Trained on 7 days and tested on 7 unseen days, it reached about 96% recall on medical events and 93% on attacks. Limits: the data is simulated, the attacks are hand-designed, and this is not a medical device. Built with Python, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and Streamlit. https://github.com/firdausiyamubarak-ux/AstroSentinel-NASA

References: NASA Human Research Program, Hazards of Human Spaceflight (nasa.gov/hrp/hazards) and Risks of Human Spaceflight (nasa.gov/hrp/risks).

NASA Data

We used NASA’s Human Research Program pages on the hazards and risks of human spaceflight (nasa.gov/hrp/hazards and nasa.gov/hrp/risks) to choose and model the medical events: radiation, hypoxia from elevated CO2, fever, and cardiac events. No raw NASA dataset was used, because the challenge lists none. The vitals data is simulated by our own code.

Space Agency Partner & Other Data

No space agency partner data was used. Open-source software: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, matplotlib, Streamlit. All data is simulated by our own code (simulate.py) in our GitHub repo.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to help write the simulation, attack-injection and detection code, the README. The machine-learning methods inside the project are Isolation Forest and Ridge regression. No AI-generated images or videos are used; all charts come from our own results. This is also acknowledged in the code repository README.
